blog_summary: Adrian Colyer reviews 'Learning the structure of generative models without labeled data' (Bach et al., ICML'17), a paper that extends the data programming paradigm introduced in Ratner et al. (2016). The key contribution is a method to automatically learn dependencies between labeling functions (LFs) in a generative model, rather than requiring users to manually specify them. The paper starts with a conditionally independent model where LF accuracies are estimated via stochastic gradient descent, then generalizes this to a factor graph model that captures higher-order dependencies (e.g., correlations) between LFs. The authors propose a scalable algorithm using pseudolikelihood optimization to learn the dependency structure efficiently, avoiding the computational overhead of Gibbs sampling. Theoretical guarantees show the method can recover the true dependency structure with high probability under certain conditions, and empirical results demonstrate significant speedups (100x) and reduced false positives compared to exhaustive parameter learning approaches.
paper_title: Learning the structure of generative models without labeled data
paper_abstract: Curating labeled training data has become the primary bottleneck in machine learning. Recent frameworks address this bottleneck with generative models to synthesize labels at scale from weak supervision sources. The generative model’s dependency structure directly affects the quality of the estimated labels, but selecting a structure automatically without any labeled data is a distinct challenge. We propose a structure estimation method that maximizes the `1 regularized marginal pseudolikelihood of the observed data. Our analysis shows that the amount of unlabeled data required to identify the true structure scales sublinearly in the number of possible dependencies for a broad class of models. Simulations show that our method is 100× faster than a maximum likelihood approach and selects 1/4 as many extraneous dependencies. We also show that our method provides an average of 1.5 F1 points of improvement over existing, user-developed information extraction applications on real-world data such as PubMed journal abstracts.
